## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kacchapajātaka* (Ja 273) is a story included in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional opening blurb, the Buddha recounted this narrative while residing at Jetavana to address the reconciliation of a quarrel between two courtiers or magnates of the king of Kosala, noting that the introductory circumstances had previously been related in the Second Book [SuttaCentral]. The verse incipit associated with the story is rendered as "Who is the one who brings the food" [SuttaCentral].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a Brahmin who practices austerities and enters deep meditation [Olson 2015]. The narrative features a disruptive, lascivious monkey who harasses the ascetic during contemplation and subsequently attempts to take sexual liberties with a tortoise sleeping by a riverbank [Olson 2015]. This work is one of several homonymous texts titled *Kacchapajātaka* in Pali literature, distinct from Ja 178 (the story of a tortoise attached to its drying pond) and Ja 215 (the talkative tortoise carried on a stick by geese) [Burlingame 1921; Anandajoti 2010; Olson 2015].
No cross-language parallels meeting score thresholds are reported in DharmaNexus or cataloged on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus identifies internal Pali text reuse between the canonical verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), comprising six matching segments (totaling 451 characters, notably including a passage at §2.4–3.4 aligned with commentary segments §2364–2365 at a 0.93 similarity score) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral lists five modern translations of the text across five languages [SuttaCentral].
**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§2.4–3.4 ↔ §2364–2365)
**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral entry for Ja 273 — Provides canonical collection data, title, opening blurb, framing context, and lists of translations and parallels.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus text-reuse database — Documents Pali-internal text reuse with the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā and lack of external cross-language parallels.
- [Olson 2015] Carl Olson, Indian asceticism: Power, violence, and play (2015) — Summarizes the narrative content of Jātaka 273 involving the meditating ascetic, the monkey, and the tortoise.
- [Burlingame 1921] Eugene W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends: Translated from the Original Pali Text of the Dhammapada Commentary (1921) — Clarifies homonymous Kacchapa Jātaka tales, specifically the talkative tortoise (Ja 215).
- [Anandajoti 2010] Bhikkhu Ānandajoti, Buddhist Wisdom Verses (2010) — Distinguishes Ja 178 Kacchapajātaka concerning non-attachment to home.
